title: A Reverse Address Resolution Protocol
subtitle: How a diskless workstation learns its own IP address from its hardware address.
summary: RARP lets a machine that knows only its hardware (MAC) address ask a server on the same network for its IP address. It is the mirror image of ARP and reuses ARP's packet format with two new opcodes, 3 for the request and 4 for the reply. It was designed for diskless workstations and has been superseded in practice by BOOTP and DHCP.

questions: how does a diskless computer get an ip address
what is the difference between arp and rarp
why was rarp replaced by bootp and dhcp
can rarp work across a router

tldr.problem: A diskless machine knows its MAC address but not its IP address.
tldr.mechanism: It broadcasts an ARP-shaped packet with opcode 3, and a server that holds a MAC-to-IP table answers with opcode 4.
tldr.outcome: It needs a server on every network segment and returns only an address, so BOOTP and then DHCP replaced it in practice.

today: As an address-assignment mechanism RARP is almost gone, because DHCP does that job. RARP frames do still turn up in one niche: virtualization software such as QEMU/KVM sends a RARP frame after a live migration so that switches relearn which port the virtual machine's MAC address is on. Packet analyzers such as Wireshark and tcpdump still decode RARP, and Linux still defines the ETH_P_RARP constant.

implementations.name: rarpd (BSD, Linux)
implementations.note: User-space RARP server daemons that answer requests from /etc/ethers and /etc/hosts.

implementations.note: The EtherType constant for RARP in the kernel headers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) lets a host discover its protocol address, for example its IP address, when it knows only its hardware address. It is the complement of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in RFC 826, which goes the other way and finds a hardware address from a protocol address.

The RFC's problem statement is short: network hosts such as diskless workstations often know only their hardware interface address when they boot, and "there is no standard mechanism" for finding the rest. Like ARP, RARP assumes a broadcast medium such as Ethernet.
sections.plainLanguage: The Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) lets a host find its IP address when it knows only its hardware address. ARP (RFC 826) works the other way, finding a hardware address from a protocol address. Diskless workstations often know only their hardware address at boot, and no standard mechanism existed. Like ARP, RARP assumes a broadcast medium such as Ethernet.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
Diskless workstations booted over the network and had no local disk to hold configuration, yet they needed an IP address before they could talk to anyone. The Ethernet address lives in the network card, but the IP address is assigned by an administrator and has no algorithmic relationship to it. Something had to bridge the two, and in 1984 nothing standard did.

The table compares RARP with the other options for getting an address into a machine that has no disk.
sections.plainLanguage: Diskless workstations boot over the network and have no disk to hold configuration, yet they need an IP address before they can communicate. The Ethernet address is built into the network card, but an administrator assigns the IP address and no formula links the two. In 1984 no standard method bridged them.

sections.title: Design
sections.content:
The authors list four considerations behind the design. ARP and RARP are different operations. A RARP server must keep a large database, which is hard to hold inside an operating-system kernel. Ease of implementation and little impact on existing hosts matter. And sharing code with existing software is desirable.

The result is a separate protocol at the data-link level that reuses ARP's packet format.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors gave four design considerations. ARP and RARP are different operations. A RARP server needs a large database, which is hard to keep inside an operating-system kernel. The protocol should be easy to implement and have little impact on existing hosts. It should share code with existing software. The result is a separate data-link protocol that reuses ARP's packet format.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
RARP uses exactly the packet format of ARP. For 48-bit Ethernet addresses and 32-bit Internet addresses every packet has hardware type 1, protocol type 2048 (0x0800, the Ethertype of IP), hardware length 6 and protocol length 4. That adds up to 28 bytes. The RFC leaves the RARP Ethertype "still to be assigned"; it was later registered as 0x8035, different from ARP's 0x0806.

In a request (opcode 3) the sender and target hardware address fields both hold the client's own MAC, and both protocol address fields are undefined. In a reply (opcode 4) the target protocol address carries the answer, and the sender fields identify the responder. Switch between request and reply below to see which fields change.
sections.plainLanguage: RARP uses ARP's packet format exactly. For Ethernet and IP the hardware type is 1, the protocol type is 0x0800, and the address lengths are 6 and 4, giving 28 bytes. In a request (opcode 3), the sender and target hardware fields hold the client's own MAC address. In a reply (opcode 4), the target protocol address holds the answer.

sections.title: Protocol Operation
sections.content:
RARP adds two opcodes beside ARP's 1 and 2: 3 ("request reverse") and 4 ("reply reverse"). A packet with any other opcode is undefined. As in ARP there are no "not found" or "error" packets, because several servers may be free to answer; a client that hears nothing should time out after a reasonable time.

Step through the exchange below, then put the server behind a router to see why RARP stays on one network segment.
sections.plainLanguage: RARP adds two opcodes to ARP's 1 and 2: 3 for a reverse request and 4 for a reverse reply. There are no "not found" or error packets because several servers may be able to answer. A client that hears nothing should time out after a reasonable time.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC's Appendix A sketches two ways to build a server on 4.2BSD Unix. One runs the whole server outside the kernel and needs a way to receive and send raw data-link packets, such as the CMU packet-filter pseudo driver. The other keeps a small cache of database entries in the kernel, filled from the full database kept by a user process through two new ioctls.

Classic Unix servers such as rarpd answer from the ethers(5) file, which maps a MAC address to a host name, and from the hosts file, which maps that name to an IP address. Neither file is part of the RFC; they are common practice. A server is needed on every network segment, because requests do not cross routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Appendix A sketches two ways to build a RARP server on 4.2BSD Unix. One runs entirely outside the kernel and needs raw access to data-link packets. The other keeps a small cache of database entries in the kernel, filled by a user process. Because requests do not cross routers, a server is needed on every network segment.

sections.title: What replaced it
sections.content:
RARP's limits were its own design: it works only on one broadcast network segment, and it returns just an address. BOOTP (RFC 951) moved the idea onto UDP and IP so it can be relayed between networks, and added a boot file name and extra fields; RFC 1542 clarified it. DHCP (RFC 2131) added leases and a rich set of options. Those became what machines actually use.

RARP itself has never been withdrawn: the RFC Editor's index lists RFC 903 as an Internet Standard (STD 38), so this page says "superseded in practice", not obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: RARP works only on one broadcast network segment and returns only an address. BOOTP (RFC 951) moved the idea onto UDP and IP so it can be relayed between networks, and added a boot file name. DHCP (RFC 2131) added leases and many options. RARP has not been withdrawn; the RFC Editor lists RFC 903 as Internet Standard STD 38.

items.title: Separate protocol, shared format
items.text: Same packet layout as ARP but its own Ethertype, so existing ARP code is not confused.

items.title: Data-link level only
items.text: RARP assumes a broadcast medium like Ethernet, so client and server share one network segment.

items.title: Servers hold the database
items.text: One or more hosts keep the hardware-to-protocol table, usually in a program outside the kernel.

items.title: No error packets
items.text: There is no "not found" reply because many servers may answer; a client simply times out.

fields.name: Protocol Type
fields.desc: ar$pro. Protocol address space. IPv4 = 2048 decimal (0x0800), the Ethertype of IP packets.

fields.name: HW Addr Length
fields.desc: ar$hln. Length of a hardware address in bytes. Ethernet = 6.

fields.name: Proto Addr Length
fields.desc: ar$pln. Length of a protocol address in bytes. IPv4 = 4.

fields.name: Operation
fields.desc: ar$op. 3 = request reverse, 4 = reply reverse. Opcodes 1 and 2 keep their ARP meaning.

fields.name: Sender HW Addr
fields.desc: ar$sha. In a request, the sender's own MAC. In a reply, the responder's MAC.

fields.name: Sender Proto Addr
fields.desc: ar$spa. Undefined in a request. In a reply, the responder's protocol address (a convenience, so the client may skip a later ARP).

fields.name: Target HW Addr
fields.desc: ar$tha. The hardware address being looked up. A client asking about itself puts its own MAC here, and a reply repeats it.

fields.name: Target Proto Addr
fields.desc: ar$tpa. Undefined in a request. In a reply, the answer: the protocol address of the target.

steps.title: A workstation powers on knowing only its MAC
steps.plainLanguage: The workstation powers on. It knows its own MAC address, which is built into its network card, but it has no IP address, so it cannot yet communicate.
steps.spec: A diskless host has its 48-bit Ethernet address in ROM but no protocol address, so it cannot use IP until it learns one.
steps.orig: Network hosts such as diskless workstations frequently do not know their protocol addresses when booted;
steps.why: IP addresses are assigned by people, not derived from the hardware, so the machine has to ask someone.

steps.title: It shouts a RARP request to everyone
steps.plainLanguage: The workstation broadcasts a RARP request containing its MAC address, 08:00:20:01:AB:C2, asking for its IP address. Every host on the network segment receives it.
steps.spec: The client sends opcode 3 with its own MAC in both the sender and target hardware fields; the protocol address fields are undefined. By convention the frame goes to the Ethernet broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF.
steps.orig: In the case where the sender wishes to determine his own protocol address, this, like ar$sha, will be the hardware address of the sender.
steps.why: It has no IP address and does not know where a server is, so shouting to the whole segment is its only option.

steps.title: Ordinary hosts ignore it
steps.plainLanguage: Ordinary hosts receive the request, see that it is not meant for them, and take no action.
steps.spec: Hosts that do not run RARP server software have nothing to answer with, because they hold no hardware-to-protocol table. Using a separate Ethertype also keeps the request away from plain ARP code.
steps.orig: The impact on existing systems is minimized; existing ARP servers will not be confused by RARP packets.
steps.why: Only a host that keeps the mapping table can give a useful answer.

steps.title: The RARP server checks its table
steps.plainLanguage: The RARP server looks up the requester's MAC address in its table, which lists each MAC address and the IP address assigned to it, and finds the matching entry.
steps.spec: The server looks up the target hardware address in its database to find the matching protocol address. On BSD-style systems that is traditionally /etc/ethers combined with /etc/hosts.
steps.orig: RARP requires one or more server hosts to maintain a database of mappings from hardware address to protocol address and respond to requests from client hosts.
steps.why: Someone has to keep that table up to date by hand, which was a real operational cost.

steps.title: The server sends back the answer
steps.plainLanguage: The RARP server sends a reply directly to the workstation that asked, telling it: "Your IP address is 192.0.2.1."
steps.spec: The server sends opcode 4. The target hardware address repeats the request, the target protocol address carries the desired IP, and the sender fields identify the responder. Implementations normally address the frame directly to the client's MAC.
steps.orig: ar$tpa is the protocol address of the target, that is, the desired address.
steps.why: Filling in the responder's own address pair as well may save the client a later ARP request.

steps.title: The workstation now has an IP address
steps.plainLanguage: The workstation now has an IP address and can communicate with the rest of the network, for example to load its operating system from a file server.
steps.spec: The client adopts 192.0.2.1 and carries on booting, typically by fetching a boot image over TFTP. If no reply ever arrives, it times out and asks again; the RFC leaves the interval open.
steps.orig: The sender of a RARP request packet should timeout if it does not receive a reply for this request within a reasonable amount of time.
steps.why: That is all RARP provides: no gateway, no DNS server, no boot file name. BOOTP added those.

failureSteps.title: The request dies at the router
failureSteps.plainLanguage: The broadcast request stays on its own network segment, and routers do not forward it. If the RARP server is on another network, it never receives the request.
failureSteps.spec: RARP works at the data-link level on a broadcast medium, and routers do not forward link-layer broadcasts. With no RARP server on this segment, the request is never answered.
failureSteps.orig: As with ARP, we assume a broadcast medium, such as Ethernet.
failureSteps.why: This is why BOOTP (RFC 951) was built on UDP/IP: it can be relayed across routers.

data.replacedNote: RARP is still in the standards track, but BOOTP and then DHCP took over its job in practice.
